title: Setting up a duck pool or paddling trough
subtitle: Ducks do not need a pond. They need enough water to submerge their head. A rubber trough drains and scrubs; a garden pond does not.
excerpt: A rubber feeding trough 45 cm deep and 60 cm long gives a pair of ducks enough water to bathe, preen, and clear their nostrils without creating an unmanageable maintenance situation. Ponds look right but are impossible to keep clean enough for the water quality ducks need. Here is how to set up a trough-based water system that works at any scale.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Ducks. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), waterfowl section. RSPCA duck welfare guidance. British Waterfowl Association housing and husbandry notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process by which ducks draw oil from the uropygial gland at the base of the tail and spread it through the feathers using the bill. Waterproofs the plumage. Ducks preen after bathing. Without access to deep enough water for bathing, feather condition deteriorates.

content.text: Ducks need water deep enough to submerge the whole head, not just the bill. This enables

and clears debris from the nostrils. A duck denied this develops sinusitis and eye problems over weeks. A rubber stock trough, large dog bath, or purpose-made duck bath meeting the minimum 45 cm depth satisfies the requirement without the maintenance burden of a pond.
Minimum depth: 45 cm for Khaki Campbells and Call ducks; 60 cm for Muscovies and large breeds such as Pekin or Aylesbury.

Tip: a container the ducks can get in and out of easily is better than a tall container that requires a ramp. Ducks do not climb well; a step in of 20-25 cm is manageable, any higher needs a ramp secured beside the container.
A drainable container is essential. A drainage bung or tilting capability makes daily changes feasible. Fixed ponds are cleaned weekly at best, which is inadequate for duck water quality.

Site the trough on a raised gravel or hardcore base so that drain-off water disperses rather than pooling. Duck water fouled with mud, wet feed, and feathers runs off across the run and makes surrounding ground boggy within days if not managed. A 60 cm apron of coarse gravel around the trough absorbs most of the splash.

Position away from the main sleeping area and the chicken feeder if running a mixed flock. Ducks splash water from the trough while bathing; a soaked chicken feeder causes feed to mould and wastes significantly.
Empty the trough daily, or twice daily in warm weather. Algae and bacterial growth in fouled duck water happens fast and causes bill infections.
Rinse the container with clean water before refilling. A scrub brush removes the film of algae and feed residue that builds on the trough walls within 24 hours.
Refill with fresh water. The ducks will use the trough within minutes.

Duck bathing water freezes before drinking water in cold conditions because the ducks keep the drinking water slightly warmer through use. In a freeze, break the ice and refill the trough with warm water twice daily. Ducks in full plumage can continue bathing even in winter; do not restrict bathing access for warmth. The uropygial oil they spread from bathing is what maintains the waterproofing that keeps them warm.
